thread.title: The Most Frowned Upon Asset May Prove The Best Investment, Again

author: Global Opportunities Analyst
title: The Most Frowned Upon Asset May Prove The Best Investment, Again
text:
Contrarianism is all about doing what the vast majority of other investors/traders consider either stupid or dangerous. Over time it has proved to be a good strategy, if combined with some decent fundamental analysis. Usually, it is not the lack of decent analysis that does not let us invest in a contrarian way but rather being seen as an idiot, or missing out on what almost everyone else has been making money on. Being contrarian is indeed tough. Let me give an example. I went long GBPUSD and EURUSD back in early 2017 when holding euros and sterling was seen as outright stupid, and closed the euro bet when confidence in the euro and the eurozone was very high, despite all the real and troubling fundamental issues that had not, and have not, gone away in Europe. It was tough, but it paid off.
What is seen as the stupidest investment at this moment? I think buying US treasuries can easily be considered the stupidest major investment idea right now. The trend of US treasuries losing favor to riskier investments is a pretty old one. It has just reached extreme levels. According to a recent survey of fund managers, done by Bank of America Merrill Lynch, short bets against US treasuries was the second most crowded trade. The most popular bet was for long positions of the largest tech stocks such as Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ), Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ), etc. Despite treasuries having recovered some of the selloff that had taken the 10-year US debt yield above 3%, the 10-year is still not far from those levels, yielding 2.90% as of last Friday, June 1 st .
But why is buying US treasuries considered such a stupid investment? Is it because it is yielding less than other investments? The S&P 500 is currently yielding around 1.85% while the 10-year US bond is yielding 105 basis points more. That is more than a full 1%. Therefore, an unattractive yield is not the reason. Is it that inflation will rise so much that it will destroy the purchasing power of the US dollar? That is indeed a hypothetical, real, threat. If inflation will pick up significantly over the coming years, that will indeed be bad for US treasuries. It will also be bad for companies and consumers. The Fed has, over the past decades, proved to be quite serious in respecting their mandate for preserving price stability - which according to them means an inflation target of 2% . This means that in case inflation will show significant strength, to overshoot the Fed target of 2%, they will not hesitate to raise rates more aggressively. That will, no doubt, keep inflation under control. Currently, the 10-year US bond yields 2.9%. This means that it is reasonable to assume that you will get 0.9% of risk-free, real, return for the coming decade. That is not great, but it isn't exactly the stupidest thing one can do either.
The only reason US treasuries seem to be considered such awful investments at the moment seems to be psychological rather than anything else. Investing in stocks is considered to be such a sure bet that investing in something which can only make you 2.9% a year is simply seen as stupid. After all, stocks have offered amazing returns for the past 9 years. And, as usual, investors tend to believe that past years continue repeating themselves.
Of course, there is also the fear investors face that if they buy treasuries, the current borrowing spree of the US government will, as a simple rule of demand and supply, push treasury prices lower in order to attract sufficient funds. I see this fear as unfounded. Although the US government has started increasing its spending, which has already raised borrowing significantly, the effects have already been priced in. The US government will need to borrow around $1 trillion a year for 2018 and, probably, for the coming two years at least. Will this push yields much higher? Not exactly. Let's not forget that it is not just US citizens who buy US debt. US debt has demand from all around the world. As US treasury yields have soared, the rest of the world has also faced some changes and challenges. The US has managed to suck in money from the rest of the world. This has therefore caused the US dollar to strengthen. In an isolated world, without the possibility of money flows, a significant increase in borrowing by the US could have indeed pushed up prices and interest rates in a much more dramatic way. However, that is not the case. The massive increase in US spending is unlikely to push inflation and treasury yields much higher, but it is going to put significant pressure on the rest of the world to scramble for both public and private funding. This has already started happening and it will likely continue, and intensify. I believe that the recent currency crises that happened in Turkey and Argentina are just the beginning. As the US will continue borrowing more, it will hold long-term interest rates elevated, while the Fed will need to keep its promise and raise short-term interest rates at least a few more times. All this will increase the pressure particularly on the weakest links of the world debt markets. If other countries will fail to keep up and raise the interest rates they offer, their currencies will be punished.
And it is not just about relatively small currencies. The increase in US borrowing has pushed the US dollar higher against all the world's other major currencies as well. The EURUSD has fallen from a high of about 1.25 earlier this year to less than 1.17.
I don't believe that the current massive borrowing from the US government will crash longer dated US treasuries, as the Fed will make sure that inflation does not get out of control. However, it will keep strengthening the US dollar and pushing up borrowing costs significantly in other countries.
The pressure will continue to build up as the whole world is swimming in both public and private debt. Global debt has kept its usual pace of hitting records . Much higher debt to GDP, especially among governments which got used to cheap money after the last financial crisis a decade ago, will mean the continuous scramble for cash will put significant upward pressure on interest rates in the rest of the world. As the economy continues to do well in the US and there is no major sign which could derail the current consumption and investment binge, the Fed will need to raise rates further, putting additional pressures on other countries and their currencies. It is very difficult to say when this pressure will be too much and a strong dollar will become unbearable, and the current economic cycle which has been expanding since 2009 will come to an end. But in a world addicted to debt accumulation, both public and private, rising short-term borrowing costs will put an ever-increasing pressure on economies all around the world. This huge amount of debt and the delicate balance between inflation and short-term funding needs will keep the lid on longer-dated US treasury yields. Hence appears the feared flattening of the yield curve (the difference between short-term and longer-dated US treasuries) that hasn't exactly reached its limits yet. It became negative just before recessions in 1990, 2000 and 2007. However, it is not an exact science yet as it hasn't really worked in Japan where interest rates have been much lower for decades.
Although the Fed was able to raise rates to 5% or more before previous economic downturns, as it can be seen in the chart below, this time around it will be very unlikely the Fed will be able to raise rates to such elevated levels. There is simply too much debt around, both public and private, not just in the US but also all around the world. The market, because of a generalized increase in debt levels, has been unable to handle higher rates, hence the trend of lower peaks just before every recession.
No matter how you look at it, US treasuries seem to be a pretty good bet against a recession which is, after all, inevitable. In case there would be a recession either in 2019 or in 2020, the Fed would need to take its overnight rates to zero again, and the 10-year US bonds would rise significantly in value, offering investors a very nice reward in an environment of falling risk assets. For example, if an investor buys the 10-year US bond now, and recession hits one year from now, he would make almost 2.9% from the yield, and if the market yield for 10-year would go down to 1%, the value of the investment would rise by 17.1% (9 years X 1.9% yield differential), offering a total return of 20%. That doesn't sound like a stupid investment at all. Missing out on a potential rise in some historically expensive stocks, which are very popular right now, would not seem so stupid either.
Of course, there is also the risk that yields keep on rising to, let's say, 4% or even higher. That would probably require the economy to keep going strong for two or three years more before the next recession. That is a possibility too, which would mean that the economy will be strong enough in the US and the rest of the world to be able to handle Fed Funding rates of around 4% in the longest running economic expansion in modern history. It can never really be ruled out, but it is a reasonable assumption that the world's record debt levels will not be able to handle funding rates that used to be applied in the 1990s and before. Here is one chart , from 2017, showing how debt levels have risen in the world, and there aren't really any exceptions.
Government debt and corporate debt are far higher than they used to be just before the financial crisis ten years ago. This is really why significantly higher interest rates are less likely to come. And this is why longer dated US treasuries can actually be some of the best investments one can make at this moment, no matter how tough it is to go against the crowd.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
